claims.claim: At least 136 wolves were killed inside Yellowstone National Park between 1914 and 1926 under the predator-control campaign.
claims.episode_span: park rangers and hired hunters killed or trapped at least 136 wolves inside Yellowstone boundaries
claims.source_title: A Timeline of the Yellowstone Wolf Reintroduction — Greater Yellowstone Coalition
claims.supporting_quote: At least 136 wolves are killed in Yellowstone National Park

claims.claim: The last official killing of wolves in Yellowstone took place in 1926, near Soda Butte Creek.
claims.episode_span: The last resident pack was eliminated in 1926 near Soda Butte Creek.
claims.source_title: History of wolves in Yellowstone - Wikipedia
claims.supporting_quote: the last official killing of wolves in the park took place in 1926 when two pups found near Soda Butte Creek were killed by park rangers

claims.claim: In 1995 and 1996, 31 wolves captured in Alberta (14) and British Columbia (17) were released in Yellowstone; 10 more from northwest Montana followed in 1997.
claims.episode_span: In 1995 and 1996, 31 wolves captured in Alberta and British Columbia were released in the park.
claims.source_title: Wolf Restoration in Yellowstone: Reintroduction to Recovery (U.S. National Park Service)
claims.supporting_quote: In 1995 and 1996, and only in Yellowstone in 1997, 76 wolves from Alberta, British Columbia, and northwest Montana were released into central Idaho and Yellowstone: 41 in Yellowstone (14 from Alberta, 17 from British Columbia, 10 from northwest Montana)

claims.claim: In the absence of wolves, coyote populations in Yellowstone increased dramatically, suppressing smaller prey such as pronghorn.
claims.episode_span: the absence of wolves also allowed coyotes to increase, which in turn suppressed smaller prey populations
claims.source_title: History of wolves in Yellowstone - Wikipedia
claims.supporting_quote: Without wolves, coyote populations increased dramatically which adversely impacted the pronghorn antelope population.

claims.claim: With wolves gone, growing elk herds overgrazed deciduous woody vegetation such as aspen in Yellowstone.
claims.episode_span: Heavy browsing prevented willow and aspen regeneration along the Lamar and Gallatin rivers
claims.source_title: History of wolves in Yellowstone - Wikipedia
claims.supporting_quote: The elk were multiplying inside the park and deciduous, woody species such as aspen and cottonwood suffered from overgrazing

claims.claim: Beaver colonies in Yellowstone increased markedly after wolf reintroduction (from one colony in 2001 to nine by 2011).
claims.episode_span: willow and aspen began recruiting again in some drainages, and beaver colonies increased
claims.source_title: History of wolves in Yellowstone - Wikipedia
claims.supporting_quote: where there was just one beaver colony in Yellowstone in 2001, there were nine beaver colonies in the park by 2011

claims.claim: The ecosystem-wide effects of removing and restoring Yellowstone's apex predator are a textbook example of a trophic cascade.
claims.episode_span: an effect biologists would later label a trophic cascade
claims.source_title: History of wolves in Yellowstone - Wikipedia
claims.supporting_quote: The top-down effect of the reintroduction of an apex predator like the wolf on other flora and fauna in an ecosystem is an example of a trophic cascade
